1:
Eliphaz opens his first speech afresh with a challenge that is half invitation and half taunt, daring Job to find one who will answer — "to which of the saints wilt thou turn?" — and the witnesses divide over both the summons to call and the "holy ones" to whom it points. The reformed John Gill weighs three senses of "call now": if seriously and not ironically spoken it is good advice, for God is to be called upon in times of trouble, in faith and with confession of sin; yet Eliphaz insinuates that if Job called it would be in vain, going on the maxim that "God heareth not sinners." Or the words bid Job call for an oracle or vision from heaven to confute what Eliphaz had delivered as revelation — which no true revelation would contradict — or else "call over" the whole catalogue of good men from the beginning to find one so dealt with.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears a fair motion to put the dispute to arbitration: so assured is Eliphaz of his cause that he lets Job himself choose the arbitrators. "If there be any that suffer as thou sufferest" — can Job name one real saint reduced to such extremity? "If there be any that say as thou sayest" — did ever a good man curse his day as Job did? "To which of the saints wilt thou turn? Turn to which thou wilt, and thou wilt find they are all of my mind": Eliphaz claims the communis sensus fidelium, the unanimous vote of the faithful, on his side.

On the identity of the saints the other schools press a different reading. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke takes the whole as strong irony — from whom among those whose foundations are in the dust canst thou expect succour? — and reads "the saints" as the holy ones (kedoshim), angels or beings as dependent on God as Job himself: neither angel nor saint can help unless sent from God, so all prayer to them is foolish and impious; "can the channel afford me water, if the fountain cease to emit it?" The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the line "to whom of the holy ones wilt thou turn?" and fix the sense: the "holy ones," as in Psalm 89, are the angels, and no cry addressed to them can avail. John Wesley keeps to the other track — call the saints by name, and not one of the children of God will defend Job's bold expostulations, though fools and wicked men might. Charles Ellicott simply marks the tone: the speaker turns personal and direct, insinuating that Job is "unwise" and "silly," and promising swift destruction to all such. So the verse leaves a real division — whether the "saints" are the godly men whose verdict Eliphaz claims, or the angels to whom Job is mockingly bidden turn in vain.
2:
The proverb Eliphaz lays down — that wrath kills "the foolish man" and envy slays "the silly one" — the witnesses take as the pivot of his argument, and they part chiefly over whose wrath does the killing. The reformed John Gill first fixes the "foolish man": not an idiot destitute of common sense, but a wicked man void of divine and spiritual knowledge, such as Eliphaz took Job to be; and the wrath is twofold. It may be the wrath of the Lord, as the Targum reads, revealed from heaven upon the children of disobedience, which consumes like devouring fire; or the wrath and passion of such men themselves, rising to such a height that they die in a fit of it, or do the things that bring them to death by the hand of God or the magistrate.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lays the whole weight on the man's own passion: the sin of sinners tends directly to their own ruin. "Wrath kills the foolish man" — his own wrath, and therefore he is foolish for indulging it; it is a fire in his bones and blood, enough to put him into a fever, and "envy is the rottenness of the bones," slaying the silly one that frets himself with it. So it is with thee, says Eliphaz: while thou quarrellest with God, thy anger at thy troubles and thy envy at our prosperity do but add to thy misery. Job had told his wife she spoke as the foolish women; now Eliphaz tells him he acts as the foolish men.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet to the same effect — "for he is a fool who is destroyed by complaining, and envy slays the simple one" — binding the death to Job's own fretting and murmuring, and setting it under the oracle's governing thought that God is the absolutely just One, exalted above men and angels. The wesleyan-arminian voices weigh it as a maxim of experience. Adam Clarke notes that "foolish," "silly," and "simple" are Solomon's own epithets for transgressors — a parallelism some have urged as evidence that Solomon wrote the book — and reads the saying thus: the wrath of God is manifested only against the wicked and impious, and were Job not such, God would not contend with him. John Wesley agrees that a man's wrath and impatience prey upon his spirit, hasten his death, and provoke God to cut him off; the foolish is the rash, inconsiderate man, and Eliphaz means, "I perceive thou art full of envy at wicked men who seem happier than thou, and of wrath against God — and this shows thee foolish." The division is real but narrow: whether the killing wrath is God's kindled judgment or the sufferer's own consuming passion, the witnesses agree that the verb is aimed, pointedly, at Job.
3:
Eliphaz now grounds his doctrine in personal observation, claiming to have "seen the foolish taking root" only to curse his habitation on a sudden; and the witnesses trace how the boast conceals a barb aimed at Job. The reformed John Gill explains the concession folded into the verse: Eliphaz had seen wicked men prosper, increase in riches, and attain a seeming stability and firmness, as if they would continue so for ever. By granting this he obviates the obvious objection to his thesis — that the wicked are notoriously not in trouble as other men, but flourishing; yes, he answers, for a while, but in a short time they and their substance pass away and are seen no more.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the "taking root" as the false security of the worldly: planted, fixed, and, in their own and others' apprehension, likely to continue. The outward estate may flourish, he warns, but the soul cannot prosper that takes root in the earth. As for the cursing, Henry is careful: Eliphaz "cursed it, suddenly cursed it, as soon as he saw them begin to take root" — not that he prayed for their ruin ("I have not desired the woeful day") but that he plainly foresaw and foretold it, going as it were into the sanctuary to understand their end (Ps. 73:17-18), for the prosperity of fools destroys them (Prov. 1:32).

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the confession the same way: "I well knew, from God's manner of dealing, that they must soon be blasted; I even ventured to pronounce their doom, for I knew that in the order of God's providence that was inevitable." John Wesley glosses each term — the foolish is the wicked man; the root, not only present prosperity but a seeming future security; the suddenness, a ruin coming in a moment beyond his own and all men's expectation; and "cursed" means, "I saw by the event which followed that he was a man accursed of God." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the verb: "I cursed" means "I was able to declare distinctly, and I did declare without hesitation, that his lot would be as follows." And Ellicott names the sting that runs beneath all these general results of experience — the insinuation that they hold the key to Job's own condition, that there is some secret unsoundness in him which is the cause of his open misery, so that a man so stricken can only be, for some unknown reason, the guilty victim of the righteous wrath of a just judge. The witnesses thus agree that the cursing is not imprecation but prognostication, and that the whole verse is a knife turned quietly toward the man on the ash-heap.
4:
"His children are far from safety" — and the witnesses feel at once how nakedly the words touch Job, whose own children had just died, and how variously the crushing "in the gate" may be read. The reformed John Gill takes the safety in several registers: the children of the foolish are far from outward safety, exposed to men who hate them for their father's sake and to God who visits the fathers' iniquity upon them, and far too from spiritual and eternal safety — "salvation," as the Targum renders it, in the world to come — since they tread in their fathers' steps and imitate their deeds.

On "crushed in the gate" the readings diverge. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes it to the seat of justice: their ill-gotten posterity shall not continue in prosperity, "ill gotten, ill spent," and they are crushed in the gate — the court and tribunal that in Eastern cities sat at the city gate, where magistrates attended and plaintiff and defendant came for judgment; the Targum even reads "bruised in the gate of hell, in the day of the great judgment." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott proposes another sense of the verb: "rather, perhaps, they crush one another," so that their own internal rivalries and dissensions bring them to ruin, and they exemplify the house divided against itself.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry keeps closer to the literal picture, and to Job's wound. The children thought themselves safe in their eldest brother's house, but were far from safety, "crushed in the gate" — perhaps the gate or doorway of the house, highest built, fell heaviest upon them, and there was none to deliver them from perishing in the ruins. He allows the common application too — that the families of wicked men are crushed by the execution of justice upon them, to make them restore what they ill-gotten, or by oppression, none helping them (Ps. 109:9). John Wesley reads the same undertone plainly: these are the children whose greatness the foolish man had designed in all his enterprises, supposing his family established for ever, yet now exposed to calamities and unable to preserve either themselves or their inheritance; "there is no question," Wesley adds, "but he glances here at the death of Job's children." So the witnesses read one verse three ways — crushed at the bar of justice, crushed by their own feuds, or crushed under a falling house — but all hear in it Eliphaz pressing his finger, however cruelly, on the freshest of Job's griefs.
5:
The picture of the ruined estate is thick with textual knots — a harvest devoured by the hungry, snatched "even out of the thorns," the substance swallowed by a spoiler — and the witnesses work at both its imagery and its disputed words. The reformed John Gill reads it of the foolish rich man who takes root and flourishes: though he sows and reaps and fancies goods laid up for many years, he is taken away by death, and another eats what he gathered — his hungry heirs, kept bare, or the poor whom he oppressed, driven by hunger to seize his harvest. He records Sephorno's turn, that the wicked man eats his own harvest yet is never satisfied, the curse of God being on his land, and another learned reading that the curse so blights his fields that they yield no more than is usually left for the poor.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sees possessions gained by unjust means abandoned by God's providence to be pillaged by "the wandering half-starved hordes of the desert banditti," who in their rapacious hurry carry off grain, weeds, and thistles together. On the last clause he presses the Hebrew: "the robber swalloweth" is more properly "the thirsty" (tsammim), plain from the swallowing or gulping down, and set in contrast to "the hungry" — so that the hungry eat the grain and the thirsty drink down the wine and oil, here called their "strength." He finds two allusions in the verse: to the predatory Arabs of the desert, whose meagre life he illustrates at length, and to Job's own cattle carried off by the Sabeans.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott makes the picture more pointed by taking the wicked man himself as the subject: he shall eat his harvest famishing and have to snatch it from among thorns — there shall be so little of it, and that little choked with briers. The word "robber," he suggests, is perhaps rather "a trap, or snare"; and he notes that some of the old versions, using other vowels, read "the thirsty swallow up," which completes the parallelism with "the hungry." John Wesley keeps it concrete and personal: the harvest they confidently expect to reap after all their cost and labour, but of which they are sadly and suddenly disappointed; "the hungry Sabeans eat it up," and take it out of the fields in spite of every danger. The witnesses thus agree on the ruin but genuinely divide on the wording — whether the last spoiler is "the robber" of the received text or "the thirsty" that Clarke and Ellicott prefer for the sake of the parallel.
6:
With his tone softening toward counsel, Eliphaz turns to a governing principle: that affliction "cometh not forth of the dust," nor trouble out of the ground; and the witnesses weigh both the sense of the line and a lexical ambiguity buried in it. The reformed John Gill reads the opening particle as "for" or "indeed," making the line a reason why the wicked are justly afflicted: their troubles come not from the creatures, though these be instruments, but from God for the sins of men. He notes that the word for "affliction" also signifies iniquity or sin — the cause as well as the fruit — so that Aben Ezra and others take both clauses of moral, not natural, evil; and Gill draws the guard that sin does not come from God the Maker of the dust, for he is not the author of sin, nor does it spring out of the ground he made, out of which come rather the good things given for the use of man and beast.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the same double reading. Taken of affliction, the verse teaches that no trouble comes by chance or by a chain of second causes: it does not spring up of course, at set seasons, as the grass does, but comes according to the will and counsel of God, when and as he thinks fit. Taken the other way — "Sin comes not forth out of the dust, nor iniquity of the ground" — it teaches that if men be bad they must lay the blame not on the soil, the climate, or the stars, but on themselves. Henry binds both together: we must not attribute our afflictions to fortune, for they are from God, nor our sins to fate, for they are from ourselves; the former is a reason to be very patient, the latter to be very penitent.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke drives the argument straight at Job, hearing in the verse the insinuation Eliphaz never quite drops: "if there were not an adequate cause, thou couldst not be so grievously afflicted." Affliction and trouble come not from mere natural causes, but from the justice of God inflicting them upon offending man. So the witnesses converge on the great principle — that suffering is no accident of the ground but the ordered dealing of God — while dividing, gently, over whether the "affliction" that does not sprout from the dust is the trouble sent or the sin that draws it down; and Clarke lets the reader feel how that principle, true in itself, is being bent into a charge against a guiltless man.
7:
"Yet man is born unto trouble, as the sparks fly upward" — the famous line, over whose last clause the witnesses divide sharply. The reformed John Gill takes "born unto trouble" as born by God's appointment for sin: as all men are appointed to death, so trouble springs from the birth-sin of man, from original corruption, the fountain from which flow all the disorders of body, the distresses of mind, and death corporeal, spiritual, and eternal that are the lot and inheritance of the sons of men; the word, he notes, carries the force of labour, mischief, and moral evil at once.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sharpens the doctrine: man is brought to trouble "not as man — had he kept his innocency he would have been born to pleasure — but as sinful man, as born of a woman (ch. 14:1), who was in the transgression." Being born in sin, he is born to trouble; and actual transgressions are the very sparks that fly out of the furnace of original corruption, so that our troubles rise as naturally and as thick as sparks fly upward. Henry marks the margin's alternative too — "man is born to labour," sentenced to eat his bread in the sweat of his face — and asks why then we should be surprised at afflictions as strange, when they are but what we are born to.

Here the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke breaks from the others on the Hebrew. "Born unto trouble," he says, is le-amal, "to labour"; and "as the sparks fly upward" is really "the sons of the coal lift up their flight, or dart upwards" — and who are these sons of the flame but bold, intrepid, ardent, fearless men, who rise superior to their trials and combat what men call chance and fortune? "I prefer this," he writes, "to all the various meanings of the place," and cites Coverdale's older turn, "It is man that is borne unto mysery, like as the byrde for to fle." John Wesley, with Henry and Gill, keeps the traditional image: man is so commonly exposed to troubles as if born to no other end, affliction being natural to him and transmitted from parents to children as their constant inheritance for sin — coming "as naturally and as generally as the sparks of fire fly upward." The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch keep the received rendering as well, reading the whole as designed to bring down man's haughtiness. So the verse leaves a genuine crux: whether it likens man's inborn trouble to the upward flight of kindled sparks, or, with Clarke, summons the "sons of the flame" to rise fearless above it.
8:
Against Job's quarrelling Eliphaz sets his own counsel of resort — "I would seek unto God," and unto God commit the whole cause — and the witnesses read it as advice edged with reproof. The reformed John Gill hears the emphatic Hebrew — "truly, certainly, I do seek unto God" — as Eliphaz describing his own practice under afflictions, for he too had them, though not to Job's degree; when they came, this was his course, to seek God by prayer to support, sanctify, and deliver him. He proposes it for Job's imitation: nothing is more proper for a saint under God's hand than to seek his face and favour, to submit and humble himself, acknowledge his sins, and implore pardoning mercy, that he may know it is in love and not in wrath that God afflicts him.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the "surely I would" of the original as a tacit reproof to Job for quarrelling with God instead of seeking him: "if I had been in thy case, I would not have been so peevish and passionate." Yet it is good and seasonable advice, which Eliphaz wisely transfers to himself as a figure; we should give our friends no counsel we would not take ourselves. The seeking is twofold: by prayer we fetch in mercy and grace, addressing God as the Father and fountain of all consolation even while he contends with us — "Is any afflicted? let him pray; it is heart's-ease, a salve for every sore" — and by patience we commit our cause to him, spreading it before him and leaving it in his hand: "Here I am, let the Lord do with me as seemeth him good."

The wesleyan-arminian voices press the same submission. Adam Clarke puts it bluntly: "were I in your place, instead of wasting time and irritating my soul with useless complaints, I would apply to my Maker, and, if conscious of my innocence, would confidently commit my cause to him." John Wesley reduces it to its parts — "if I were in thy condition," seek God "by prayer, and humiliation, and submission, imploring his pardon and favour." The witnesses do not divide over the substance, and only faintly over the grammar — whether Eliphaz says what he does in his own trials, as Gill hears it, or what he would do were he in Job's place, as Henry, Clarke, and Wesley take it. Either way they agree the verse turns from accusation toward invitation: the God who is said to afflict is the very God to whom the afflicted must carry his cause.
9:
Eliphaz begins to magnify the God to whom he has just bidden Job resort, the One who "doeth great things and unsearchable," and the witnesses gather up the several ranges of those marvels without number. The reformed John Gill sorts them into three: the great things of creation, when the heavens and earth and all their host were made out of nothing by the word of the Almighty; the great things of providence, in upholding all things, governing the universe, and supplying every creature; and, above all, the great things of grace — the covenant and its blessings, redemption by Christ, and the work of grace on the heart that takes away the stony heart and gives one of flesh. To consider all this, he says, is a great encouragement to seek the Lord in time of need.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry expounds the three epithets that describe God's power. It is unsearchable — the works of nature are mysterious, the wisest philosophers own themselves at a loss, and the designs of providence are deeper still (Eccl. 3:11; Rom. 11:33); it is numerous, doing great things without number, a power never exhausted; and it is marvellous, such that eternity itself will be too short to admire it. By pressing this, Henry says, Eliphaz means both to convince Job of his folly in quarrelling with a God whose works are above our judgment and who can crush us in a moment, and to encourage him to seek One to whom such power belongs, who can do great things for our relief when we are brought ever so low.

The wesleyan-arminian voices strike the same double note. Adam Clarke: "no work, however complicated, is too deep for his counsel to plan; none, however stupendous, too great for his power to execute; he who is upright is always safe in referring his cause to God." John Wesley explains that Eliphaz here launches into a discourse on the infinite perfection of God's nature and works precisely as an argument to enforce his exhortation — for God is able either to punish Job far worse if he keeps provoking him, or to raise him from the dust if he humbly addresses him; and by displaying the vast disproportion between God and Job, to convince him of his great sin in speaking so boldly and irreverently. Even the "marvellous" things, Wesley adds, though common and therefore despised, are matter of wonder to the wisest men. The witnesses do not divide: the greatness of God is set out at once as a rebuke to Job's presumption and as a ground for his hope.
10:
For his first instance of God's great works Eliphaz names the falling rain, given "upon the earth" and sent upon the fields, and the witnesses linger over how large a wonder hides in so common a gift. The reformed John Gill widens the scope against the older Jewish reading: not upon the land of Israel only, as the Targum and Jarchi took it, but upon the whole earth. Rain is peculiarly of God — none of the vanities of the Gentiles can give it — and it is a free gift that tarries not for the desert of men, bestowed on the godly and the ungodly alike, a great blessing of goodness that enriches the earth and makes it fruitful for man and beast.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps the Chaldee's narrower turn for its beauty — "who gives rain on the face of the land of Israel, and sends waters on the provinces of the people" — and hears in it the very truth of our Lord's word that the Father "sendeth rain on the just and on the unjust" (Matt. 5:45). On the second clause he presses the Hebrew: the word rendered "fields" (chutsoth) generally means streets, and may here signify the cultivated plots laid out in ridges, so that God not only rains upon the earth at large but by a special providence waters the tilled ground, that not one ridge lack its due share of fructifying moisture. John Wesley marvels that Eliphaz should open with so ordinary a work, and finds the wonder in it — the strange rising of the water from the earth, the hanging of that heavy body in the air, and its distribution as God sees fit; and if there be such mystery in the rain, how much more in the hidden paths of divine providence.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the lesson: "he gives rain upon the earth" stands for all the gifts of common providence, the fruitful seasons by which God fills our hearts with food and gladness (Acts 14:17). When Eliphaz would show what great things God does, Henry observes, he instances the giving of rain, which, because it is a common thing, we are apt to reckon a little thing; but if we duly consider both how it is produced and what is produced by it, we shall see it to be a great work of power and goodness. Too often, he adds, the great Author of our comforts and the manner in which they are conveyed pass unnoticed, only because they are received as things of course. The witnesses do not contend — save over the Targum's Israel-only limit, which Gill rejects and Clarke keeps for its aptness — and together they make the falling rain a standing proof of the God who does great things unsearchable.
11:
The reversal that God's providence works — setting "on high those that be low," and lifting the mourners to safety — the witnesses read both literally and figuratively, as rain raising the poor husbandman and grace raising the humble. The reformed John Gill offers the plainer, agricultural sense first, tying the verse to the rain just named: not the low plants that shoot up under the showers, but the husbandmen and gardeners in low circumstances, whose lands the rain makes fruitful, so that they are raised to good estates and large possessions. The blessing that waters the field lifts the poor man who tills it.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it of God's impartial bounty: he so distributes his providential blessings without partiality that the poor man's land is as well sunned and watered as the rich man's, and thus he is set upon a level with the lords of the soil. John Wesley takes it more broadly still as "he setteth up" — another example of God's great and wonderful works, given here to comfort and encourage Job to seek God, "because he can raise him out of his greatest depths."

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott draws out the doctrine of the line: man's exaltation must come from God, and not from his own vain strivings — a truth he ranges alongside the great reversals of Scripture, the song of Hannah and the psalmists who sing that the Lord puts down and lifts up (1 Sam. 2:6-8; Ps. 75:4-10; Ps. 113:7). The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears the same music and gives it its fullest voice: those whom proud men contrive to crush God raises from under their feet and sets in safety; the lowly in heart and those that mourn he advances, comforts, and makes to dwell on high in the munitions of rocks; Zion's mourners are the sealed ones, marked for safety. And Henry binds this verse to the next, seeing in it the very theme of Mary's song — that God has scattered the proud in the imagination of their hearts and exalted them of low degree (Luke 1:51-53). The witnesses do not divide over the truth, only over its reach: whether Eliphaz points first to the poor farmer lifted by the rain, or straight to the humble and the mourning whom God is pleased to raise; and all of them turn it, as Eliphaz means it, into an argument for Job to abase himself and be exalted in due time.
12:
As the counterpart to his lifting of the low, Eliphaz declares that God "disappointeth the devices of the crafty," so that the same providence which raises the humble baffles the scheming; and the witnesses attend to who does the disappointing. The reformed John Gill records a striking minority reading before his own — that some Jewish commentators make the subject not God but the rain, so that the shower which falls upon the earth disappoints the crafty who in a drought withhold their corn to enhance its price and grind the poor, forcing them to bring it out and sell it cheap, and so taking them in their own craftiness; and the Targum applies the verse to the Egyptians, whose cunning devices against Israel came to nothing. But the plain drift is God's own disappointing of the wily.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gathers the sweep of it: all these sayings refer to the particular providence of God, ever working for the good and counterworking the plots of the wicked; and as various as are the contingent, capricious, and malevolent acts of men, so varied are his providential interferences, disappointing their devices, snares, and plots, so that their machinery is broken in pieces and their hands cannot perform. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott tightens the last clause: rather than "cannot perform their enterprise," it is that "their hands can do nothing that is sound or of worth, can accomplish nothing effectual" — the craft comes to a barren end.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the verse its theatre of history. There is a supreme power, he says, that manages and overrules men who think themselves free and absolute, and fulfils its own purposes in spite of their projects. The froward who walk contrary to God are often very crafty, being the seed of the old serpent noted for his subtlety; they think themselves wise, but at the end will be fools. They have their devices and confederacies against the kingdom of God and its faithful subjects, restless and unwearied, high in hope and deep in policy; and God can, and so far as is for his glory certainly will, blast them all. Henry rolls out the roll of ruined plots — how the counsels of Ahithophel, Sanballat, and Haman were baffled, and the confederacies gathered against Israel broken — so that the hands stretched out against God and his church have never performed their enterprise. The witnesses converge on the comfort in it for a sufferer: the God who is able to overthrow the mightiest schemer is the God to whom Job is bidden commit his cause.
13:
"He taketh the wise in their own craftiness" — a line the witnesses treasure both for its picture of self-snared cunning and for the singular honour the New Testament pays it. The reformed John Gill paints the trap: as beasts are taken in a pit and birds in a snare, so crafty men, wise in their own conceit, are entangled in their own schemes and fall into the pit they dug for others — Haman hanged on the gallows he built for Mordecai — or are taken "by their own craftiness," the very means they use bringing about what they meant to prevent, as Joseph's brethren, selling him to defeat his dreams, fulfilled them.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott records the verse's great distinction: "St. Paul quotes the former half in his warning to the Corinthians — 'The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God; for it is written, He taketh the wise in their own craftiness'" (1 Cor. 3:19). He glosses "froward" as crooked, perverse, or tortuous, noting that the name Naphtali springs from the same root (Gen. 30:8). Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet to match — "who catcheth the wise in their craftiness, and the counsel of the cunning is thrown down."

The wesleyan-arminian voices supply the proverb-lore. Adam Clarke observes that God so counterworks the crafty that their feet are taken in their own snares and their evil dealings fall on their own pate, so that "he who digs a pit for his neighbour shall fall into it himself" has become a universal adage; and he quotes Lucretius, that "force and wrong entangle the man who uses them, and recoil on the head of the contriver." John Wesley reads "the froward" as wrestlers, who wind and turn every way and leave no means untried, yet are "carried headlong," tumbled down and broken by their own precipitation. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the same lesson and the same apostolic seal: that which enemies designed for the ruin of the church has often turned to their own ruin, for "he takes the wise in their own craftiness"; and this, Henry notes, "is quoted by the apostle (1 Cor. 3:19) to show how the learned men of the heathen were befooled by their own vain philosophy." The witnesses do not divide; they rejoice together that a saying of Eliphaz, however misapplied to Job, was owned by Paul as canonical Scripture, and stands for ever as the epitaph of every cunning that outwits itself.
14:
The snared schemers of the last verse are now struck blind in the plainest light, made to "meet with darkness in the daytime" and to grope at noon as in the night; and the witnesses read the stroke as judicial. The reformed John Gill reads the darkness as infatuation in things most clear and obvious, so that the greatest politicians, men of the sharpest sagacity, blunder in what is easy to the meanest capacity — given up to a judicial blindness by the Lord who destroys the wisdom of the wise; or it is the defeat of their counsels when these are most esteemed, as Ahithophel's counsel was once reckoned an oracle of God, or their destruction in the very meridian of their glory.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke describes the same confounding: God so confuses them and their measures that, for all their cunning and dexterity, they are outwitted and act upon their well-laid plans as if these were the crudest conceptions of disordered minds; they move in the noonday "as if the sun were extinct, and their eyes put out." Thus, he says, does God abate their pride, assuage their malice, and confound their devices. John Wesley reads the darkness here not as misery but as ignorance and error: in plain things they run into gross mistakes and choose the courses worst for themselves, groping like blind men to find their way, not knowing what to do.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds a philological and historical note. The phrase, he thinks, is possibly an allusion to the Egyptian plague of darkness "that may be felt" (Exod. 10:21), the words being similar — perhaps a mark of the book's date; and he compares Isaiah 59:10, where the thoughts correspond though the words differ. This is one of the many passages of Job, he observes, in which there seems some acquaintance with the events related in the Pentateuch, though the points of contact are too slight for us to be quite sure of it. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sums the whole: when God infatuates men they are perplexed and at a loss even in things most plain and easy — "they meet with darkness in the day-time," nay, as the margin has it, they run themselves into darkness by the violence and precipitation of their own counsels. The witnesses do not divide; they leave the crafty stumbling at noon, a warning that the God Job is urged to seek can dim the brightest human wisdom in an instant.
15:
Turning from the confounded schemers to their intended victims, the verse declares that God "saveth the poor" from sword and mouth and the hand of the mighty; and the witnesses work at a genuine knot in its Hebrew. The reformed John Gill reads the poor in a literal sense: they are the very butt of the crafty, on whom the cunning fix their eyes and lay their snares; being helpless and without friends, they are the ones God takes notice of, appears for, and saves with a temporal salvation.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke finds the received phrase harsh — "from the sword, from their mouth" — and turns to the manuscripts: eleven of Kennicott and De Rossi's copies read "from the sword of their mouth," and with them agree the Chaldee, Vulgate, Syriac, and Arabic. So he would render, "He saveth from the sword of their mouth the poor, from the hand of the mighty," or "He saveth from the sword of their mouth, and with a strong hand the impoverished." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott treats it as a matter of grammatical nicety — whether the sword is conceived as coming forth from their mouth, or as identical with what comes from it, or as the first of three distinct things from which the poor are delivered. But he lifts the eye from the grammar to the wonder: it is worthy of special note, he says, that the Lord is here conceived and represented as the Saviour, and the Saviour of them who have no saviour — an idea confined, or at least pre-eminently characteristic, to the circle of the sacred writings.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the verse its pastoral force: the designs of the crafty are to ruin the poor, and tongue and hand and sword and all are set to work for it; but God takes under his special protection those who, being poor and unable to help themselves, and being his poor, devoted to his praise, have committed themselves to him. He saves them from the mouth that speaks hard things against them and the hand that does hard things against them; for he can, when he pleases, tie the tongue and wither the hand. The witnesses do not divide over the mercy, only over the syntax that carries it — whether the poor are snatched "from the sword of their mouth," as Clarke's manuscripts read, or from sword, mouth, and mighty hand in turn — and all of them hear in the line the note that Ellicott prizes most, God as the Saviour of the helpless who have none else to save them.
16:
The paragraph on providence closes with a twofold fruit of the deliverance just described — hope kindled in the poor and helpless, and iniquity itself made to "stop her mouth" — and the witnesses take the two effects together as one movement. The reformed John Gill lets the poor man reason from what he sees: observing this and that afflicted one crying to the Lord and saved, he hopes he too may be saved; and having himself known deliverance out of one trouble or more, he entertains a comfortable hope of being brought through the next. The word, Gill notes, signifies one weak and feeble, attenuated, exhausted of his strength and substance — which he applies also to the spiritually poor and forlorn, who through the revelation of grace has hope of safety in Christ, the strong hold set before him.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes the same term: "the poor" (dal) is he who is made thin, wasted, extenuated; and he has hope because he sees what God is accustomed to do and expects a like dealing for himself. And because God deals thus with those who trust him, "the mouth of impiety is stopped"; religion, Clarke adds, is kept alive in the earth by God's signal interventions on behalf of the bodies and souls of his followers. John Wesley reads the closing clause of the wicked directly: "iniquity" is wicked men, who are silenced and confounded, finding that not only are the poor got out of their snares, but the oppressors themselves are ensnared in them.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott anchors the phrase in its Scriptural echo, noting that "iniquity stoppeth her mouth" recurs word for word in Psalm 107:42. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the two effects together: weak and timorous saints are comforted, for the poor who began to despair now has hope, since the experiences of some are encouragements to others to hope the best in the worst of times — it being the glory of God to send help to the helpless and hope to the hopeless; and daring, threatening sinners are confounded, for iniquity stops her mouth, surprised at the strangeness of the deliverance, ashamed of its enmity against the favourites of heaven, and compelled to acknowledge the justice of God's proceedings, having nothing to object. The witnesses do not divide; they close the paragraph on providence with the poor lifting up their heads and wickedness struck dumb.
17:
"Happy is the man whom God correcteth" — the great hinge of Eliphaz's close, about which the witnesses crowd, weighing both its comfort and its exact wording. The reformed John Gill distinguishes the kind of correction meant: not the sentence of a judge condemning malefactors, but the discipline of a father correcting his children, in love, in judgment, and in measure, for faults committed. God corrects by his word, which is profitable for reproof, by his ministers sent to rebuke, by his Spirit convincing of sin, and by afflictive providences — the rod he uses with his children — to bring them to repentance and to wean them from over-valuing the creature.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry expounds the paradox: "happy is the man whom God correcteth," if he make but a due improvement of it. A good man is happy though afflicted, for whatever he has lost he has not lost his enjoyment of God nor his title to heaven; nay, he is happy because afflicted, for correction mortifies his corruptions, weans his heart from the world, and draws him nearer to God, bringing him to his Bible and to his knees (Jam. 1:12). Therefore, Henry urges, "despise not the chastening of the Almighty" — call it a chastening, from a father's love and for the child's good; be not averse to it, think not ill of it, nor overlook it as chance, but reverence it as the voice of God. And he notes, weighing the friend's whole speech, that as Paul quoted v.13 for canonical Scripture and the command of this verse binds us still, these promises may be received as divine.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds a rich textual observation: this verse is probably the original of Proverbs 3:12, which is itself quoted by the writer to the Hebrews (Heb. 12:5), its spirit echoed by James and by John in the Revelation; and this is the only place in Job where the word for "happy" — the very first word of the Psalter, used five-and-twenty times there — is found. Keil and Delitzsch render "happy is the man whom Eloah correcteth" and mark the turn: the speech now becomes persuasive as it moves toward its conclusion, since the God who humbles the self-exalting humbles in order to raise. The wesleyan-arminian voices confirm both text and doctrine. Adam Clarke notes that "behold" is wanting in several manuscripts and versions, and appeals to the argument that if we submitted to the fathers of our flesh who corrected us, how much more to the Father of spirits, who chastens that we may partake of his holiness (Heb. 12:5). John Wesley hears the plural in the Hebrew — "blessednesses" belong to the man God rebukes — and draws from it that the ancients already held the hope of everlasting blessedness, without which the promise could not be true; "despise not," he says, means do not abhor it as pernicious, refuse it as useless, or slight it as needless, but reverence the correcting hand. The witnesses do not divide: chastening is a father's love, and the man under it is, rightly seen, a happy man.
18:
"For he maketh sore, and bindeth up" — the ground of the beatitude just pronounced, and the witnesses dwell on the tender surgery of a God who wounds only to heal. The reformed John Gill reads the couplet with a concessive force — "though he maketh sore, yet he bindeth up" — and draws out the image of the surgeon who makes a wound the sorer by probing and opening it, to let out the matter and make way for the medicine, and then lays on the plaster and binds it up. So God causes grief by diseases of body, by breaches in families and estates, and then heals the stroke of the wound; and so too in spiritual things, wounding by the two-edged sword of the word and Spirit, laying open the corruption of nature and bringing to repentance, and then pouring in the oil and wine of pardoning grace.

The grammatical-historical witnesses keep close to the wording and its weight. Keil and Delitzsch render it, "for He woundeth, and He also bindeth up; He bruiseth, and His hands make whole." Charles Ellicott owns the sentiment to be one of those obvious ones that lose all their force from familiarity, yet which come home sometimes in sorrow "with a power that is boundless, because Divine." The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke prizes the old English of Coverdale, who rendered the verse nervously: "For though he make a wounde, he giveth a medicyne agayne; though he smyte, his honde maketh whole agayne."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry brings the doctrine to its point of comfort. Though God makes sore the body with boils and the mind with sad thoughts, he binds up at the same time, as the skilful and tender surgeon binds up the very wounds he had occasion to make with his knife; when he makes sores by the rebukes of his providence, he binds up by the consolations of his Spirit, which often abound most as afflictions abound. His usual method, Henry says, is first to wound and then to heal, first to convince and then to comfort, first to humble and then to exalt — and, as he quotes, "the hand that inflicts the wound applies the cure." Never does God make a wound too great, too deep, for his own healing (Hos. 6:1). The witnesses do not divide; they hold up one God who both smites and saves, so that the same hand Job feels heavy upon him is the hand appointed to make him whole.
19:
Eliphaz opens his string of promises with a pledge of unfailing rescue — deliverance "in six troubles," and in seven no evil touching him — and the witnesses read the numbers, the tense, and the bitter irony together. The reformed John Gill makes the deliverance conditional on the behaviour just urged — seeking God, committing the cause to him, not despising the chastening — and takes the "six" and "seven" as a certain number put for an uncertain, God delivering out of whatsoever troubles may come. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke agrees that six and seven stand for many: though a number of troubles come at once and there be, humanly speaking, no hope, God would rid Job of them all, for he saves from many as readily as from few; and the words may also mean that he who has been thy deliverer in past troubles will not deny his help in those to come. John Wesley applies it directly to Job — deliverance, "if thou seekest to him by prayer and repentance" — reads the "six" as manifold and repeated, and the "touch" as touching so as to destroy, promising a good issue out of all his troubles though they be both great and many.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends to the form and its sting. The numerical figure of speech — six, yea seven — is characteristic mainly of the Proverbs (Prov. 6:16), a manner of the wisdom writers; and since evil was at that very moment emphatically touching Job, "the actual irony of these words must have been bitter indeed." The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the comfort while granting the recurrence of trouble: as afflictions recur, supports and deliverances shall be graciously repeated, be it ever so often, for as long as we are in this world we must expect a succession of troubles, the clouds returning after the rain; after six may come a seventh, but out of them all God delivers his own, former deliverances being not, as among men, excuses from further help but earnests of it (2 Tim. 3:11). And the promise that "no evil shall touch thee" means, Henry says, that the malignity and the sting are taken out — troubles may hiss but cannot hurt, for the evil one toucheth not God's children (1 John 5:18). The witnesses do not divide over the sense — repeated, unfailing rescue for the man who seeks God — yet Ellicott will not let the reader miss how heavily the fair words fall on a man already, in his own flesh, touched by the seventh trouble.
20:
The promises grow particular as Eliphaz pledges redemption "from death" in famine and from the power of the sword in war, and the witnesses note both the wonders behind them and a quiet question of tense. The reformed John Gill reads it of God's special care in extremity: in a time of extreme want he so provides for his own that they are not starved to death, as in the famines of Abraham's, Isaac's, and Jacob's days food was found for them and their households; God sometimes goes out of his ordinary way and works wonders for his poor and needy in distress when they cry to him.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps the Chaldee's reading of the whole chapter as the story of Israel's troubles and deliverances: "in the famine of Egypt he redeemed thee from death, and in the war of Amalek from the slaying of the sword." John Wesley uses the verse to expose the ground on which Eliphaz speaks so confidently. He utters these things, Wesley says, with the more assurance because under the Old Testament the rewards and punishments of this life were more constantly distributed according to men's behaviour than they are now; and because it was Eliphaz's fixed opinion that great afflictions were the certain evidences of wickedness, and that great deliverances would infallibly follow upon true repentance — a premise that, applied to Job, was as false as it was confident.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses a nicety of the verb: it is rather "he hath redeemed thee," as though the speaker could appeal to Job's own past experience of God's rescues, which itself becomes a ground of confident hope for the future. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the promise into its comfort: when desolating judgments are abroad, God's people are taken under special protection. Do many perish for want of the necessaries of life? They shall be supplied — "in famine he shall redeem thee from death"; whatever becomes of others, thou shalt be kept alive, satisfied even in the days of famine (Ps. 33:19). And in time of war, when thousands fall on the right hand and the left, he shall redeem thee from the power of the sword; if God please it shall not touch thee, and if it wound or even kill the body, it cannot hurt, having no power but what is given from above. The witnesses do not divide over the mercy; they differ only over whether Eliphaz points forward to deliverances promised or, with Ellicott, back to redemptions Job had already known — and Wesley alone lifts the veil on the flawed doctrine that made the friend so sure.
21:
Among the perils from which the man shall be kept, Eliphaz names the "scourge of the tongue," from which he shall be hidden, and destruction, which he shall not fear; and the witnesses dwell on the peculiar cruelty of slander. The reformed John Gill takes the "scourge of the tongue" of the slanders and calumnies of wicked men — Jarchi refers it to Satan the accuser — and marks how small a weapon does how much harm: the tongue is like a scourge or whip, cutting though little, as Jeremiah's enemies smote him with their tongue. God hides his people from it, either restraining men's tongues, laying as it were an embargo on them, or so overcharging the slander that none will credit it, so that the good man's character stands.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke pours out the whole catalogue of the sin. The Targum refers the promise to the incantations of Balaam — "from the tongue of Balaam thou shalt be hidden in the clouds, and thou shalt not fear the blasting of the Midianites" — and Clarke reflects that perhaps no evil is more dreadful than the scourge of the tongue: evil-speaking, detraction, backbiting, calumny, slander, tale-bearing, and whispering, the works of that member which is "a world of fire, kindled from the nethermost hell." Scripture, he notes, abounds with invectives against it (Ps. 52:2-4; Jam. 3:1-8). And of the second clause he says the sense is that a man should have such strong confidence in God that even in the presence of destruction he should not fear death, the God of life and power being with him.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott briefly ties the fear here to the language of v.15, keeping the paragraph knit together. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the promise its balance: thou shalt be hidden from the scourge of the tongue, which like a scourge is vexing and painful though not mortal; the best and most inoffensive men cannot, even in their innocency, secure themselves from calumny and false accusation, from which a man cannot hide himself — but God can hide him, so that the slanders neither disturb his peace nor blemish his reputation, and God restrains the remainder of wrath. So too they shall have a holy security of mind, not afraid of destruction even when they see it coming. The witnesses do not divide; they leave the sufferer covered, under God's hand, from the one weapon that innocence cannot parry for itself.
22:
"At destruction and famine thou shalt laugh" — a promise of holy fearlessness that crowns the string of assurances, and the witnesses are careful to define the kind of laughter Eliphaz means, lest it be mistaken for scorn. The reformed John Gill guards it from scorn: not that the man derides or makes a jest of God's judgments, for good men have a reverence and awe of them, but that amid such calamities he reckons himself safe and secure, provision being made for his protection and sustenance, and so is cheerful and at peace, trusting in the Lord as Habakkuk did when every necessary of life was cut off (Hab. 3:17) — like a man in a good harbour, who laughs at the storms and winds that rage about him.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it as the strongest security and the fullest confidence in that security, and keeps the Targum's colouring: "in the desolation of Sihon, and in the famine of the desert, thou shalt laugh; and of the camps of Og, who is compared to a wild beast of the earth, thou shalt not be afraid." John Wesley strikes the same note: the laughter is "a laughter of joy and triumph, arising from a just security and confidence in God's watchful and gracious providence." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the second clause literally — "and of the beasts of the earth be not thou afraid" — keeping its imperative force.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry lifts the fearlessness to its height. They shall not be afraid of destruction when it comes, nor of the beasts of the field when they set upon them, nor of men as cruel as beasts; nay, "at destruction and famine thou shalt laugh" — not despising God's chastenings or making a jest of his judgments, but triumphing in God, in his power and goodness, and therein triumphing over the world and all its grievances, to be not only easy but cheerful and joyful in tribulation. So, Henry says, blessed Paul laughed at destruction when he cried, "O death, where is thy sting?" and defied all the calamities of this present time to separate us from the love of God, concluding that in all these things we are more than conquerors (Rom. 8:35). The witnesses do not divide; they only take care, with Gill, that the saint's laughter is the calm of trust and not the sneer of presumption.
23:
The peace promised the man reaches even to nature, so that he stands "in league with the stones of the field" and at truce with its beasts; and the witnesses divide over what those stones are and how the league is struck. The reformed John Gill takes them as literal field-stones, with which the man shall be so at league that he receives no hurt walking among them, even barefoot, as was usual in the east; or so that they hinder not the increase of his crops, since even stony ground may yield a large harvest, and the stones serve as useful boundaries and landmarks not to be removed. He records the ingenious sense of Pineda, drawn from an Arabian custom he calls Scopelism — the laying of stones in an enemy's field to threaten any who should till it — from which the promise frees him.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sets out the alternatives fully. Mr. Good would read not abney (stones) but beney (sons or produce) of the field, though no version or manuscript supports it; the Chaldee turns it, "thy covenant is on tables of stone publicly erected in the field, and the Canaanites, compared to beasts of the field, have made peace with thee"; and Clarke himself inclines to see the "stones" as the rocks and strongholds where banditti or the neighbouring chieftains had their seat, so that, instead of preying on Job as the Sabeans did, "the castles in the land shall be confederate with thee," as Coverdale rendered it, and even the beasts shall not be permitted to harm his flocks.

The grammatical-historical voices keep to the plainer construction. Charles Ellicott renders it literally, "for with the stones of the field shall thy covenant be, and the beasts of the field shall be made to be at peace with thee," and Keil and Delitzsch read it the same way, "thou art in league with the stones of the field, and the beasts of the field are at peace with thee." The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the theology of the league: when a man is at peace with God there is a covenant of friendship between him and the whole creation, so that walking over his grounds he need not fear stumbling on the stones nor be in danger from the beasts; while man is at enmity with his Maker the inferior creatures are at war with him, but "a reconciled God reconciles all things" (compare Hos. 2:18). John Wesley calls it a bold metaphor, an addition to the former privilege — the creatures shall not merely spare but befriend him — and sums it: our covenant with God is a covenant with all the creatures, that they do us no hurt but be ready to serve us. So the witnesses agree on the peace and divide on the picture — literal stones at truce, or strongholds and chieftains turned allies.
24:
From the fields Eliphaz turns to the household, promising that the man shall "know that his tabernacle shall be in peace" and shall visit his habitation without loss; and the witnesses part over the closing verb. The reformed John Gill takes the "tabernacle" not as a place of worship, nor as the frail tent of Job's own diseased body, but as his dwelling-house, built like a tent as the eastern houses were, movable for the sake of pasturage — such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob dwelt in — and including his household; so that, behaving aright under the afflicting hand, his family should be in peace.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws out both the Hebrew and the scene. The man shall be so satisfied of the friendly disposition of all his neighbours that he shall rest secure in his bed, and returning from his country excursions shall find his habitation preserved and shall have made no mistake in his trust. Clarke distinguishes the two words — "tabernacle" (ohel) a movable tent, and "habitation" (naveh) a solid, permanent dwelling — and reads "shalt not sin" (techeta, from a root meaning to err, to miss the mark) most likely as "thou shalt make no mistake"; for the Arab chiefs, on their excursions, were sometimes attacked in their absence and their households carried off. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses the same point: the word rendered "sin" literally means to miss the mark (as in Judges 20:16), and probably means so here — "thou shalt visit thy dwelling-place, and miss nothing" — since one does not readily see why a promise of not sinning should be tied to visiting the habitation or fold.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry keeps the moral reading and finds a wealth of family piety in it. "Peace is thy tabernacle," he renders it — peace the house in which those dwell who dwell in God; God provides his people a settlement, mean perhaps and movable, a cottage or a tent, yet fixed and quiet, so that "thou shalt not sin," or wander, that is, not be a fugitive and vagabond under Cain's curse but dwell in the land. And they shall have wisdom to govern their families and look well to the ways of their household — which is the "visiting" of their habitation — and grace to manage its concerns without sin. The witnesses do not divide over the peace promised the house, only over its last word — whether the man is promised that he shall "not sin" in his household, as Henry hears it, or that he shall visit it and "miss nothing," as Clarke and Ellicott read the Hebrew.
25:
The promise of a numerous seed, an offspring "as the grass of the earth," must have pierced the man who had buried all his children; and the witnesses handle both its words and its painful gap from fact. The reformed John Gill reads "thy seed" not of seed sown in the ground but, with Bar Tzemach, of the man's children — their greatness either in worldly things, in wealth and honour and power, or in their numbers, for the word may be rendered "much" or "many," a multitude of children being reckoned a great temporal blessing.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch note that the verse recalls the Solomonic Psalm 72:16, and that the word for "offspring" is one found in the Old Testament only in Isaiah and in the book of Job. Charles Ellicott agrees that "great" here means rather "numerous," which better suits the parallelism with the grass of the earth; and he pauses over the whole description as "a very beautiful and poetical one of the perfect security of faith," yet one "vitiated by its want of strict correspondence with facts, of which the very case of Job was a crucial instance." This, he says, was the special problem with which the friends had to deal and which proved too hard for them — and he draws the lesson that such a problem "can only be solved in practice and not in theory."

The wesleyan-arminian voices keep the promise simple. Adam Clarke glosses "thine offspring as the grass" — "thou shalt have a numerous and permanent issue"; John Wesley grounds the knowing in God's promises and the impressions of his Spirit, to be confirmed by experience in due time. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry feels the tenderness of it toward Job in particular: Job had lost all his children, but if he return to God, "he will again build up thy family, and thy seed shall be many and as great as ever, and thy offspring increasing and flourishing as the grass of the earth" — for God has blessings in store for the seed of the faithful, and it is a comfort to parents to see the prosperity, especially the spiritual prosperity, of their children. The witnesses do not divide over the words, and only Ellicott lets the shadow fall openly across the promise — that this fair doctrine of guaranteed increase broke on the rock of Job's own emptied house.
26:
"Thou shalt come to thy grave in a full age" — the last of the promises, in whose harvest-image, the shock of corn gathered in its season, the witnesses find both a gentle death and a hint of more. The reformed John Gill notes that the grave is here figured as a house to be entered and dwelt in, man's long home appointed for all the living; and since the dead do not literally go but are carried to it, the phrase must denote a willingness to die — the readiness of one who would be absent from the body and present with the Lord, giving up the ghost cheerfully and even rejoicing that the grave is near, while others have their souls required of them and are driven away in their wickedness against their will.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it as a death in due season and turns the corn-image toward resurrection: thou shalt not die before thy time, but depart from life "like a full-fed guest," happy in what thou hast known and enjoyed, having run the whole round of life's seasons, and shalt be buried "like a wholesome seed in the earth, from which thou shalt again rise up into an eternal spring." John Wesley marks that "full age" means a mature and old but still vigorous age; it is a great blessing to live to a full age and not have one's months cut off in the midst, much more to be willing to die, to come cheerfully to the grave, and to die seasonably, "just in the bed-time, when our souls are ripe for God."

The grammatical-historical witnesses supply the philology and the finer contrast. Keil and Delitzsch explain the rare word for "full age" as denoting the maturity of old age, connected with a root meaning to be completed, and set it against the parallel image of the sheaves brought up to the high threshing-floor at the latest period of harvest. Charles Ellicott hears, not improbably, a deliberate contrast between going down into the grave and going up to the barn, so that the grave is "not the melancholy end of life, but rather the passage to a higher life for which one is already ripe" — and he sets over it the apostle's words, "henceforth there is laid up for me a crown of righteousness" (2 Tim. 4:8). The witnesses do not divide; they gather the whole promise into a death without terror — the corn cut only when fully ripe, and, for Clarke and Ellicott, gathered not to rot but to rise.
27:
Eliphaz seals his speech by claiming that all he has said has been "searched" and proved — "so it is" — and the witnesses weigh both the confidence of the conclusion and its misapplication. The reformed John Gill explains the appeal: to engage Job's attention, Eliphaz observes that what he has said is not his single opinion but the shared sentiment of his friends, and the fruit of laborious inquiry — they had searched the records of former times, questioned the ancient, and observed the course of things through their own lives, and so are agreed that "so it is." The bidding "know thou it for thy good," Gill adds, is a call to lay the whole to heart and profit by it, as truth diligently searched out is a treasure worth the digging.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it as the sum of Eliphaz's wisdom and experience, "established maxims which universal experience supports"; "know" means understand and reduce them to practice for thy good. Thus ends Eliphaz, Clarke says, "full of wise saws and ancient instances" — yet he "miserably perverted them in his application of them to Job's case and character," though the sayings themselves contain many wholesome truths of which the wise in heart may make advantageous use. John Wesley catches the same self-assurance without the censure: "this is no rash or hasty conceit, but what both I and my brethren have learned by deep consideration, long experience, and diligent observation"; and "know thou it" for thyself, with application to thy own case, for that which we so hear and know for ourselves we hear and know for our good.

The grammatical-historical voices name the flaw more sharply. Keil and Delitzsch mark that the speech of Eliphaz, ranged in its several strophes, here closes with an epimythion — a summing moral tacked to the whole. Charles Ellicott fastens on the tone: "it is the boastful confidence of Eliphaz which is so hard to bear. He speaks as though Job's experience were as nothing to his — 'This is mine: take it to thyself, and make it thine.'" The witnesses do not finally divide: they agree that the maxims gathered here are, in the main, true and even weighty, and that the fault lies not in the doctrine but in the delivery — a first speech ending, for all its wisdom, in a confident thrust at a man whose case it did not fit, and whose deeper trouble it never touched.
